title: The maid who welcomed the sage
hook: the younger widow turns pale, the elder sends her maid instead, and the maid's welcome gives the palace its wisest son
carry: atithi devo bhava: the guest is god
tomorrow: a princess learns her groom is blind, and takes a vow.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Ambika shut her eyes, and Dhritarashtra was born blind. Moha: the blindness of 'mine'.

Same palace, same sage, a different widow. Satyavati sends Vyasa to the younger princess, Ambalika. When she sees him, the blood leaves her face. She doesn't shut her eyes, as her sister did; her fear shows on her face instead. And the Kuru house is about to get three brothers: the blind one, the pale one, and one nobody planned for at all.
screen: `A DIFFERENT WIDOW.` → `SHE GOES PALE.` → `ONE NOBODY PLANNED FOR.`

segments.voice: Vyasa tells his mother: because she turned pale, the son will be pale. Pandu, the pale one. Satyavati asks for one more son from the elder widow. But Ambika can't face him again. She dresses her maid in her own jewels and sends her instead. The maid isn't afraid. She rises when the sage comes in, greets him with respect, and serves him. Vyasa is pleased. You are no longer a servant, he tells her, and your son will be virtuous and wise. That son is Vidura, and the text later says he is Dharma itself, the god of what's right, born as a man. So, three brothers: one who can't see, one who's pale, and the wisest, born to the woman everyone else overlooked. Hindus have a name for what she did. Atithi devo bhava: let the guest be God to you. It comes from the Taittiriya Upanishad, part of a teacher's parting advice to students, beside honoring mother, father and teacher. The princesses saw a frightening stranger. The maid saw someone to honor, and her life changed. Many teachers read it this way: the welcome itself is worship. That's why, in many Hindu homes, a guest gets water before asking, the best seat, and the first plate, even unannounced, even when there's little to give. Today it's the friend who drops by and leaves full, or the new kid you wave over to your table. In this tradition, how you greet the one at your door is part of how you greet God.
screen: `PANDU, THE PALE ONE.` · `THE MAID RISES AND GREETS HIM.` · `VIDURA, DHARMA BORN AS A MAN.` · `THE WELCOME ITSELF IS WORSHIP.` · then, large: `ATITHI DEVO BHAVA: THE GUEST IS GOD.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind who might come to your door this week: a friend, a neighbor, a relative you find hard. Picture greeting them the way the maid did: standing up, a glass of water, a real hello. If you pray, offer a little water or food at your altar or in your heart first, as many Hindus do before eating. If you don't, just choose one small welcome you'll give.
Pandu, the pale one, born because his mother's face went white; brother to the blind Dhritarashtra and the wise Vidura.
Your line: atithi devo bhava, the guest is God. A maid's welcome gave the palace its wisest son. Day seven hundred twenty-three, done.

howItsDone: Atithi devo bhava, from the Taittiriya Upanishad, is still taught to Hindu children and lived at the door: water first, the best seat, a full plate. Vidura's later counsel, the Vidura Niti, is read by some Hindus as a guide to wise living.

notes: All paraphrase. Confirm in Ganguli: Ambalika's pallor and Vyasa naming the son Pandu for it; Ambika's substitution of her maid adorned in her ornaments; the maid's respectful welcome; Vyasa freeing her from servitude and praising the coming son; Vyasa telling Satyavati of the deception.
Vyasa's blessing on the son is softened to 'virtuous and wise'; Ganguli's wording is stronger and was not used under the no-superlatives rule.
Vidura as an incarnation of Dharma under Animandavya's curse is only mentioned, not told.
The maid is described as a Sudra woman in the text; the script says 'servant' and 'mother's place'. A Keeper may wish to address caste more directly or not at all.
howItsDone names the Vidura Niti; confirm placement in the Udyoga Parva and phrasing.
